summary: This informational document clarifies many areas of the IKEv2 specification without changing the protocol, giving descriptions that are less prone to ambiguity, to encourage interoperable implementations. It was replaced by RFC 5996.

plainLanguage.summary: The rule book for setting up secure connections had confusing parts. This explains them again more clearly without changing the rules. It was later replaced by RFC 5996.

subtitle: Clarifications and implementation guidance for the IKEv2 key exchange protocol.

tldr.problem: IKEv2, the protocol for establishing secure connections, had ambiguous sections that could lead to different implementations and interoperability failures.
tldr.mechanism: This document clarifies confusing areas without changing the protocol itself, covering initial setup, authentication, security association negotiation, rekeying, edge cases, and configuration.
tldr.outcome: The clarifications help developers build compatible IKEv2 implementations. RFC 5996 later consolidated IKEv2 and some clarifications into a unified specification.

today: RFC 4718 is an Informational document that was superseded by RFC 5996. RFC 5996 consolidated the IKEv2 specification and incorporated many of these clarifications into the main specification text. Modern IKEv2 implementations should follow RFC 5996 or later.

sections.title: Clarifying the IKEv2 Specification
sections.content:
IKEv2 is the protocol that two computers use to agree on how to set up a secure tunnel (an IPsec tunnel) for encrypted communication. The original specification was sometimes unclear about what should happen in corner cases or ambiguous situations. This document addresses those areas without changing the protocol itself.

The clarifications come from mailing list discussions, interoperability testing, and real implementation experience. The document uses IKEv2 for remote-access VPNs, site-to-site VPNs, and host-to-host protection, but focuses especially on remote-access scenarios where one machine connects to a VPN gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: IKEv2 sets up secure tunnels between computers. Some parts of the rules were hard to understand, so this document explains them again more clearly without changing how they actually work.

sections.title: Setting Up the Initial IKE_SA
sections.content:
When two computers first connect, they exchange messages to create an IKE_SA (a security association for the key exchange protocol itself). The initial exchange, called IKE_SA_INIT, has several corner cases.

One issue concerns Security Parameter Indexes (SPIs), which identify the connection. In the first message of IKE_SA_INIT, the responder's SPI is always zero because no security state has been created yet. When the responder sends back a cookie or rejects the proposal, it should still use zero for the responder SPI, because no state has been allocated on the responder's side.

Another clarification covers Message IDs: during IKE_SA_INIT, all message IDs are zero, even when retrying due to cookies or invalid key exchange payloads. Message IDs only start counting from 1 after the initial exchange completes. Additionally, when the responder receives an IKE_SA_INIT request, it must distinguish between a retransmission of an existing request and a brand new request. The RFC recommends using the whole packet hash or at least the Nonce payload for this lookup, rather than just the initiator's SPI.
sections.plainLanguage: When two computers first start talking securely, they have to exchange some special numbers. The IKEv2 rules explain what numbers to use in different situations, like when one computer asks again because it didn't hear back.

sections.title: Authentication and Key Negotiation
sections.content:
The next critical phase after IKE_SA_INIT is the IKE_AUTH exchange, where the two computers prove who they are. The document clarifies how authentication payloads are calculated, how hash functions are chosen for signatures, and how different identity types work with different authentication methods.

One key clarification: when using RSA signatures, the protocol does not negotiate which hash function to use. The signing party chooses the algorithm. The document recommends using SHA-1 as the default unless there is a good reason to use something else. When using shared-key authentication, PRFs (pseudo-random functions) with fixed key sizes are problematic and should be avoided, because the shared secret must exactly match the PRF's required key size.

Another important point concerns EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) authentication. When EAP is used, the IDi payload may be used only for routing to the AAA server, not for actual authentication. The actual authenticated identity comes from the EAP server, and policy lookups must use that identity, not the ID payload.
sections.plainLanguage: To prove their identity, computers can sign messages or share a secret key. This explains which methods work together and how to choose the right signature algorithm so both computers understand each other.

sections.title: Creating and Managing Child Security Associations
sections.content:
CHILD_SAs are the actual security associations that protect the user's data traffic. They are created using the CREATE_CHILD_SA exchange. This exchange also handles rekeying (creating new keys) and deletion of both CHILD_SAs and the IKE_SA itself.

When creating a CHILD_SA, the initiator proposes traffic selectors (ranges of IP addresses and ports) that should be protected by the SA. The responder may narrow these to match its policy. The document clarifies how narrowing works: if the responder's policy allows only a subset of what the initiator proposed, the responder narrows to an acceptable subset that includes the first selector proposed.

CHILD_SAs always exist in pairs (one in each direction), so deletion must delete both. When rekeying a CHILD_SA, the initiator includes a REKEY_SA notification identifying which SA is being rekeyed. When rekeying the IKE_SA itself (to get fresh keys), no traffic selectors are involved, only the SA and key exchange payloads.

An important clarification: rekeying and reauthentication are different concepts. Rekeying just creates new keys; reauthentication verifies the parties still have access to their long-term credentials. IKEv2 does not have a dedicated reauthentication mechanism; instead, a new IKE_SA is created from scratch using the full authentication process.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the computers trust each other, they create tunnels (CHILD_SAs) for the real data. This explains how to set them up, refresh the keys, and clean them up when done.

sections.title: Handling Simultaneous Exchanges
sections.content:
One of the most complex clarifications covers what happens when both computers try to do something at the same time. For example, both might try to rekey the same SA, or one might try to delete an SA while the other tries to rekey it. These exchange collisions can temporarily leave the two computers with different views of what SAs exist.

When simultaneous rekeying happens, both peers initially respond as usual, creating redundant SAs. They then compare the nonces (random values) used in the two exchanges. The endpoint that created the rekeyed SA with the lowest nonce closes the redundant SA it created, and the original initiator closes the old SA. The nonce comparison uses octet-by-octet lexicographical comparison, not numeric comparison.

The document provides a detailed summary of how to handle various collision scenarios: what to do when two exchanges affect SAs that are being closed, rekeyed, or created. In general, if a host receives a request affecting an SA in an incomplete state, it replies with a notification like NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN to indicate the request cannot be processed.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes both computers try to refresh keys at the same time, creating a mess. This explains how to clean it up by comparing random numbers and deleting the extra tunnels.

sections.title: Configuration, Traffic Selectors, and Implementation Issues
sections.content:
The IKEv2 specification allows configuration of IP addresses via configuration payloads. The document clarifies that this is the only mechanism for address assignment; traffic selector payloads have different semantics and do not assign addresses. When both are present in a message, they often contain the same information, but they mean different things.

Traffic selectors have special rules for ICMP and IPv6 Mobility Header: the ICMP type and code are treated as a single 16-bit "port" field, with type in the most significant bits. Similarly, the IPv6 Mobility Header message type is encoded in the most significant 8 bits of the 16-bit port field.

The document also addresses several implementation mistakes and edge cases: how to handle invalid cookies (simply ignore them and send a new cookie), how Diffie-Hellman groups are negotiated during SA creation, how Extended Sequence Numbers (ESN) are negotiated, and how traffic selectors are narrowed when policies conflict. It recommends that when rekeying the IKE_SA, implementations should require a fresh Diffie-Hellman exchange (not allow the value NONE), as this provides stronger forward secrecy guarantees.
sections.plainLanguage: When computers are setting up secure tunnels, they need to agree on details like which addresses to protect and how to handle special types of network traffic. This explains all those details and common mistakes to avoid.
